issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s need for business premises may be sustained when the proposed business is for unemployed adult sons, alleged alternatives are not available or suitable, and the reviewing court is asked to disturb factual findings on the evidence.
material_facts: The landlord sought release of a shop so her two adult, unemployed sons could carry on business.
A shop relied on as an alternative belonged to the landlord’s sister, not to the landlord.
The District Judge found that the landlord’s other premises could not be used for the sons’ business, based on the evidence.
The tenant did not bring the sister-owned shop to the District Judge’s attention as an alternative accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The sister-owned shop could not be treated as accommodation available to the landlord, and the District Judge’s findings on the landlord’s need and the suitability of the other premises disclosed no basis for interference in writ proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, a landlord may seek release on the ground of bona fide need. Accommodation belonging to another person is not available to the landlord merely because of a family or co-ownership connection, and findings about the suitability of premises based on appraisal of evidence are essentially factual. The Court applied these principles in declining to interfere with the District Judge’s findings.

predicates.release_proceeding_for_landlord_business: A landlord seeks release of business premises for a claimed business need.
predicates.sons_unemployed_seeking_business: The landlord’s adult sons are unemployed and want to carry on business.
predicates.claimed_alternative_owned_by_relative: An alleged alternative premises belongs to a relative rather than being available to the landlord.
predicates.other_premises_found_unsuitable_on_evide: The fact-finder concludes from the evidence that the landlord’s other premises are unsuitable for the proposed business.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks business premises for unemployed sons, an alleged alternative belongs to a relative, and the other premises are found unsuitable on the evidence, the landlord’s need finding is sustained.

issues.legal_issue: Comparative hardship in a business-premises release proceeding is assessed by considering the prescribed business-related factors, including tenant occupancy, available alternative accommodation, the landlord’s existing business, and a son’s self-employment need.
material_facts: The tenant had occupied the shop since 1966.
It was undisputed that the tenant had no suitable accommodation to which he could shift.
The District Judge considered the landlord’s existing business.
The landlord’s two adult sons had completed their education, were unemployed, and wanted to carry on business for self-employment.
The District Judge’s order addressed the relevant factors for business premises under Rule 16(2).
issues.conclusion: The District Judge did not disregard Rule 16(2), and the sons’ need for self-employment was an outweighing circumstance supporting release to the landlord.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 16(2) of the Rules under the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, identifies factors relevant to comparative hardship for business premises: longer tenant occupation reduces the justification for release; suitable alternative accommodation for the tenant increases it; the landlord’s existing business is relevant; and due consideration is to be given to a son who, after completing technical education, is not in government service and seeks self-employment. Rule 16(1), which concerns residential accommodation, did not apply. The Court distinguished Bishan Chand v. Vth Addl. District Judge because the relevant business-premises factors had not been considered there and an outweighing circumstance was present here.

rule.if: business_premises_release_proceeding and tenant_long_occupancy and tenant_lacks_suitable_alternative and landlord_existing_business_considered and landlord_son_unemployed_seeking_self_employment

predicates.business_premises_release_proceeding: A landlord seeks release of premises let for business use.
predicates.tenant_long_occupancy: The tenant has occupied the premises for a substantial period.
predicates.tenant_lacks_suitable_alternative: The tenant has no suitable alternative premises to which to shift.
predicates.landlord_existing_business_considered: The decision-maker takes the landlord’s existing business into account.
predicates.landlord_son_unemployed_seeking_self_emp: A son of the landlord is unemployed and seeks to become self-employed.

issues.definition: In a business-premises release proceeding, when the tenant has occupied for a substantial period but lacks suitable alternative premises, the landlord’s business is considered, and an unemployed son seeks self-employment, comparative hardship may favor the landlord.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s claim that no alternative accommodation is available must be supported by evidence, and scarcity of accommodation is not a matter for judicial notice in deciding comparative hardship.
material_facts: The District Judge treated the hardships as equally balanced but relied on the landlord’s sons’ self-employment need as an additional circumstance favoring the landlord.
The tenant had produced no material showing that he had tried during the litigation to obtain alternative accommodation and had been unable to do so.
The tenant argued that scarcity of accommodation could be judicially noticed.
The Court held that the availability of alternative accommodation in the circumstances had to be proved by evidence.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could not rely on an unsupported assertion that alternative accommodation was unavailable, and the Court declined to take judicial notice of general scarcity of accommodation.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing relative hardship, each party must prove its relative advantages or disadvantages; the entire burden cannot be placed on the landlord to prove that the tenant’s disadvantages are remediable. The availability of alternative accommodation is a matter to be proved by evidence, not judicial notice. The Court relied on Mst. Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan, distinguished Bishan Chand v. Vth Addl. District Judge, and rejected reliance on Gautam Chand Jain v. Sushila Kumari Jain as establishing that scarcity could be judicially noticed.

predicates.business_premises_release_proceeding: A landlord seeks release of premises let for business use.
predicates.hardship_comparison_tied: The decision-maker assesses the parties’ hardships as equal.
predicates.tenant_claims_no_alternative_accommodati: The tenant asserts that no alternative accommodation is available.
predicates.tenant_offers_no_evidence_of_unavailabil: The tenant provides no evidence that alternative accommodation is unavailable or that efforts to obtain it failed.

issues.definition: When hardship is assessed as equal in a business-premises release proceeding, an unsupported claim that no alternative accommodation is available does not weigh for the tenant.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant carrying on business in premises subject to an eviction order may be granted a limited opportunity to vacate on conditions imposed by the Court.
material_facts: The tenant had been carrying on business in the shop.
The release application had been pending for many years.
The tenant requested time to vacate after the appeal was dismissed.
The Court conditioned the postponement of eviction on payment of the awarded costs and filing an undertaking.
issues.conclusion: The Court postponed enforcement of the eviction order for a limited period, subject to the tenant depositing the costs and filing an undertaking within the specified time.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its discretion to allow time for a business tenant to vacate, subject to compliance with conditions; the judgment states no separate statutory test or earlier case governing this relief.

rule.if: eviction_order_upheld and tenant_carries_on_business and tenant_requests_time_to_vacate and tenant_complies_with_court_conditions

predicates.eviction_order_upheld: An eviction order against the tenant has been upheld.
predicates.tenant_carries_on_business: The tenant carries on business in the premises.
predicates.tenant_requests_time_to_vacate: The tenant asks the Court for additional time to vacate.
predicates.tenant_complies_with_court_conditions: The tenant satisfies the conditions set by the Court for postponing enforcement.

issues.definition: When an eviction order is upheld against a business tenant who requests time to vacate and complies with the Court’s conditions, enforcement may be postponed conditionally.
